cards.explanation: The reason Paul gives is that they do the same things. Paul, who wrote this letter, says the judge is condemning himself "…because you who pass judgment do the same things." It's like me pointing at someone's crumbs while my own apron looks like a crumb parade. Wagging a finger at somebody else gets awkward fast when the same thing is sitting on your own hands.

The answer is True, friends. Paul, who wrote this letter, says, "And we know that God’s judgment against those who do such things is based on truth." No guessing and no rumors, just truth. Think of a recipe card with every measurement exactly right. I'd trust that card over my own memory any day.

God's kindness leads to repentance, friends. Paul, who wrote this letter, says "…God’s kindness leads you to repentance?" So the kindness isn't just there to be enjoyed. It's pointing somewhere, and that somewhere is turning around. I've been on the receiving end of that kindness myself, and it got me out of the back of a junk drawer.

The word is wrath, friends. Paul, who wrote this letter, says the hard and unrepentant heart is "…storing up wrath against yourself for the day of wrath…" The verse says the storing is something this person is doing, and it points to the day when God's righteous judgment will be revealed. That's a heavy line, so let's let it sit for a second.

God gives eternal life, friends. For those who keep at doing good and seek glory, honor and immortality, Paul, who wrote this letter, says "…He will give eternal life." Notice who does the giving. It's God, and He's the one handing it out. Perseverance means sticking with it, like a baker who keeps showing up even when the dough is being stubborn.

The answer is False, friends. The statement leaves the Greek out, but Paul, who wrote this letter, writes of "…glory, honor, and peace for everyone who does good, first for the Jew, then for the Greek." Everyone means everyone, so both get it. That Greek is right there in the verse, and nobody is getting left out of this batch.

The reason is that God does not show favoritism, friends. Paul, who wrote this letter, puts it plainly: "For God does not show favoritism." Jew or Greek, doing evil or doing good, the same standard holds. There's no VIP section at the front of this bakery line, and I'm glad, because I'd never make it to the front.

The word is judged, friends. Paul, who wrote this letter, says all who sin under the law "…will be judged by the law." The law is the standard they stand under. Think of me holding my own cookies up against the recipe card. Funny how the card never lies.

The doers of the law are the ones declared righteous, friends. Paul, who wrote this letter, says, "…it is the doers of the law who will be declared righteous." It isn't enough to hear the words. They have to be done. That's the difference between owning a cookie cutter and actually pressing it into the dough.

What it shows is that the law's work is written on their hearts, friends. Paul, who wrote this letter, says, "So they show that the work of the law is written on their hearts…" These Gentiles don't have the law, but the work of it shows up inside them. That's a lot closer than any piece of paper could get.

The word is consciences, friends. Paul, who wrote this letter, says, "…their consciences also bearing witness, and their thoughts either accusing or defending them" So inside each of these Gentiles there's a witness, and it's their own conscience. I think that little voice has pointed at my crumbs more than once.

God will judge men's secrets through Christ Jesus, friends. Paul, who wrote this letter, says it is "…through Christ Jesus, as proclaimed by my gospel." So Jesus is the one through whom God judges them. Paul calls it his gospel, meaning the good news he proclaims. Secrets and all, it's in the best hands.
